summary: Proposes an SDP attribute to state the RTCP port in a session. SDP assumes the ports used are consecutive, but a NAT that maps ports can break the ordering. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A video call uses two doors that are meant to be next to each other. Address swapping boxes can move them apart. This memo adds a way to say where the second door is.

questions: what is the sdp rtcp attribute
why does rtcp need its own port in sdp
how does nat break rtcp ports
subtitle: An SDP attribute that states the RTCP port explicitly, so calls still work when a NAT scrambles port numbers.

tldr.problem: SDP assumes the RTCP port follows the media port, but a NAT that maps ports can destroy that ordering and even put RTP and RTCP on different addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3605 adds a media-level attribute, a=rtcp, that carries the RTCP port and optionally a network type, address type and connection address.
tldr.outcome: Hosts behind a port-mapping NAT can state the RTCP port as it appears outside. The RFC calls this a narrow fix and expects it to become unnecessary.

today: RFC 3605 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with NATs and Ports
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is often used to set up multimedia sessions, and it describes the IP addresses and ports with SDP (RFC 2327). When a host sits behind a network address translation device, the SDP text must give the addresses and UDP ports as they appear on the public Internet side of the NAT.

Audio and video usually travel over RTP (RFC 3550), which needs two UDP ports: one for media and one for the control protocol, RTCP. SDP carries only one port per media and says the other ports should be derived algorithmically from the base media port. Older versions of RTP, such as RFC 1889, forced the RTCP port to be derived from the media port. That restriction has been lifted, so RTCP ports now need to be stated explicitly.

A NAT that does port mapping gives no guarantee that two mapped ports keep the ordering and parity of the originals. If it manages a pool of IP addresses, RTP and RTCP may even end up on different addresses. RFC 3605 uses an SDP attribute to record the RTCP port and, optionally, the address.
sections.eli5: A call needs two numbered doors side by side. A box in the middle can renumber them so they are no longer neighbors, and then nobody finds the second one.

sections.title: The rtcp Attribute
sections.content:
The rtcp attribute documents the RTCP port for a media stream when that port is not the next higher (odd) port number after the RTP port in the media line. It is a value attribute in the form a=<attribute>:<value>. The name is the lowercase string rtcp, and the value is the RTCP port number and an optional address.

The formal syntax uses ABNF: rtcp-attribute = "a=rtcp:" port [nettype space addrtype space connection-address] CRLF. The tokens port, nettype, addrtype and connection-address are defined in Appendix A of RFC 2327.

The attribute MAY be used at media level and MUST NOT be used at session level. Both unicast and multicast values are valid.
sections.eli5: The note says 'a=rtcp:' and then the number of the second door. You can also add the street address if it is different.

sections.title: Example Encodings
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples, all for an audio stream on media port 49170. The first states only the RTCP port, 53020. The second adds an IPv4 address with IN IP4 126.16.64.4. The third adds an IPv6 address with IN IP6 2001:2345:6789:ABCD:EF01:2345:6789:ABCD.

In each case the RTCP port is not the next odd number after 49170, which is exactly the situation the attribute exists for.
sections.eli5: Each example is a call whose second door is numbered something unexpected. The note tells the other side which number to use.

sections.title: Discovery and Design Choices
sections.content:
The attribute is only useful if a host can learn the translated ports, meaning the ports as seen on the external side of the NAT. One suggestion is to ask a well-connected third party acting as a STUN server (RFC 3489). The host allocates two UDP ports for the RTP/RTCP pair, sends a UDP message from each to the server, and the server copies the source address and port of each packet into a reply. The host parses the reply to learn the external address and port for each. This supposes that the NAT uses the same translation for the third party and for the SDP peer, which is not guaranteed for every NAT.

The RFC considers and rejects two alternatives. Documenting several ports per media is not needed, because layered encoding is not much used and mostly runs with multicast, while the translation issues apply only to unicast. Expanding the media line was rejected because it would be awkward and because applications that do not understand it would have to reject the whole media description. An attribute fails more gently: implementations that do not understand a=rtcp ignore it, so they fail to send RTCP to the given address but can still receive the RTP media.
sections.eli5: To find your outside door numbers you ask a helper far away what numbers it sees. The memo chose a small add-on note instead of changing the main line, because old programs can just skip a note they do not understand.

sections.title: UNSAF Considerations
sections.content:
The RTCP attribute is used to enable RTP/RTCP flows through NAT, and it can work with an address discovery mechanism such as STUN. The RFC calls STUN a short term fix, which brings in the issues of Unilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) in RFC 3424.

The attribute addresses a very specific problem, and the RFC says it SHOULD NOT be used for other applications. It expects one of two exit strategies: an explicit middlebox control protocol that lets applications obtain suitable RTP and RTCP port pairs, or the deployment of IPv6 with end-to-end addressing. Either would remove the need for a non-standard RTCP port in the attribute.
sections.eli5: This is a patch for one specific problem, and the authors hope better fixes will make it unnecessary.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is not believed to introduce any significant security risk. A malevolent third party could try to redirect the RTCP part of an RTP exchange, but that requires intercepting and rewriting the signaling packet carrying the SDP. Anyone who can do that has many more attacks available, including changing the addresses and ports of the media itself.

To guard against this, when SDP is carried as application/sdp the RFC calls for end-to-end integrity using S/MIME (RFC 3369), which is compatible with SIP. For IANA, the attribute field rtcp is a new SDP parameter that, per RFC 2327, has been registered. It is designed for use at media level only.
sections.eli5: Someone who could change the call setup note could do far worse things than move the second door, so the answer is to protect the whole note from tampering.
